opening_note: November is when San Diego's evenings finally turn. The days still reach the high sixties, but the nights drop into the fifties, and for the first time since spring an hour with a pot in the oven sounds good. The first satsumas arrive, and the cool-weather vegetables come back — leeks, fennel, chard, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts. The month cooks at two speeds: one slow pot and one soup for the weekend, and quick, crisp, bright cooking the rest of the week, from the air fryer and the wok. Everything below comes from one store and a fish market.
thesis: Keep the meal. Change the season.

field_notes.name: A loose peel is a good sign.
field_notes.body: Satsumas grow a puffy peel that comes away from the fruit; that's the variety, not age. Judge them by weight instead: pick up two of the same size and buy the heavier one. They're the reason to keep a bag in the fridge through December.

field_notes.name: A braise is a sear that keeps going.
field_notes.body: Everything October taught about the sear — dry meat, hot pan, hands off until it lets go — is the first step of a braise. Then add a little liquid, partway up, and give it a low oven and time. Leave the lid off if there's skin to keep crisp. In December, the same pot holds a pork shoulder for three hours; the steps don't change.

field_notes.name: Small batches, big heat.
field_notes.body: A home burner can't heat a wok the way a restaurant flame does, so don't ask it to cook a pound of meat at once. Get the wok smoking, cook in two batches in a single layer, and leave each one alone for a minute before you toss. Crowded, meat steams and turns gray — the same lesson as October's sear, only faster. Have everything cut and the sauce mixed before the wok goes on; there's no time to chop once it starts.

field_notes.name: The air fryer is a small, fast oven.
field_notes.body: It doesn't fry anything. It blows very hot air around the food, which is why it crisps chicken skin and Brussels sprouts better than a crowded sheet pan. The oven's rules still apply: one layer, room around each piece, a toss or a flip halfway. It runs hotter and faster than an oven recipe expects, so check early. Fat collects in the drawer; pour it off before a second batch, or it smokes.

field_notes.name: Press a mushroom like a steak.
field_notes.body: Oyster mushrooms are mostly water. Tear them into big clusters, lay them in a hot, lightly oiled cast-iron pan, and set something heavy on top — a smaller skillet, or the Dutch oven's lid with a can inside. The weight squeezes the water out so they brown instead of steam, and in about 5 minutes a side they shrink to half their thickness, crisp at the edges and meaty inside. Salt them once they've browned. It's October's sear with a weight on it.

field_notes.name: Chard stems go in first.
field_notes.body: A bunch of chard is two vegetables: stems that need five minutes and leaves that need one. Chop the stems and start them with the leeks or the garlic; tear in the leaves at the end. Thrown in together, you get stringy stems or gray leaves.

drink.name: Sherman Heights Café de Olla
drink.intro: One drink. The evenings turned, and November opens with Día de los Muertos.
drink.card_line: Coffee, cinnamon, brown sugar, satsuma peel
drink.method: Bring four cups of water to a simmer in a saucepan with the cinnamon stick, brown sugar, and satsuma peel, and let it bubble gently for five minutes so the cinnamon opens up. Take it off the heat, stir in a third of a cup of ground coffee, and let it steep for four minutes. Pour it through a fine strainer, or a paper filter if you want it clean. It should taste like coffee first, then spice, and only a little sweet. It's traditionally made in a clay pot, the olla; any saucepan works.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: A braise should barely move.
one_thing_to_notice.body: Open the oven and look at the pot. The liquid around the chicken should be shivering — a few lazy bubbles at the edges — not boiling. A hard boil tightens the meat and clouds the sauce. If it's rolling, turn the oven down twenty-five degrees. The same goes for the soup on the stove.

satsumas.name: Satsuma mandarins
satsumas.tile_uses: The jar, the weekend braise, the halibut salad, mornings, the drink
satsumas.why_now: Satsumas are among the first California citrus of the season, and they start arriving in November — sweet, seedless, and so loose in their skins they peel in one piece. They're at their best now and through December.
how_to_choose: Heavy for their size; light ones have started to dry out
A puffy, loose peel is normal for a satsuma, not a sign of age
Bright orange, with a little green near the stem still fine
No soft, sunken spots
satsumas.buy_this_much: A 2-lb bag, about ten. One goes into the jar and the braise; the rest get eaten out of hand.
satsumas.price_note: Usually sold in bags or by the pound; the bags are cheaper and just as good.

satsumas.storage: In the fridge, loose, for up to two weeks. On the counter they're fine for a few days.
satsumas.one_thing_to_learn: A satsuma's loose peel is the variety, not age. Judge them by weight instead: a heavy one is full of juice.

fennel.name: Fennel
fennel.tile_uses: The jar, the weekend braise, the halibut salad
fennel.why_now: Fennel is a cool-weather vegetable; as the nights drop into the fifties it comes back sweet and crisp. Raw, it's anise-cool and crunchy; cooked slowly, it turns soft and mild.
how_to_choose: Heavy, tight, white bulbs
No brown bruising or splitting on the outer layers
Fresh, upright fronds; limp fronds mean it's been sitting
fennel.buy_this_much: 3 bulbs: two for the jar, one for the braise. One more if you make the halibut.
fennel.price_note: Sold by the bulb. Bigger bulbs are usually the better deal.

fennel.one_thing_to_learn: Fennel changes completely with heat: raw it's crisp and cool, cooked it goes soft and sweet and loses most of its anise. Someone who doesn't like it raw may love it braised.

leeks.name: Leeks
leeks.why_now: Leeks come into their own as the weather cools. Cooked slowly, they melt into something soft and sweet that turns a braise or a soup into a cool-weather dish.
how_to_choose: Straight, firm white and light-green parts
Fresh, dark tops without yellowing
Medium leeks are more tender than very thick ones
leeks.buy_this_much: 4 for the suggested week: two for the braise, two for the minestrone.
leeks.price_note: Sold singly or in bunches of two or three.

leeks.one_thing_to_learn: Leeks hold grit between their layers. Slice them first, then swish the slices in a bowl of cold water and lift them out with your hands; the sand sinks to the bottom.

swiss-chard.name: Swiss chard
swiss-chard.tile_uses: The minestrone, the crisp chicken's white beans
swiss-chard.why_now: Chard is one of the greens that does best in Southern California's cool season. It's tender enough to cook in minutes and sturdy enough for a pot of soup.
how_to_choose: Glossy, upright leaves with no yellowing
Crisp stems that snap rather than bend
Any color — rainbow, red, or white — cooks the same

swiss-chard.one_thing_to_learn: Chard is two vegetables. The stems need five minutes longer than the leaves, so chop them and start them first; add the leaves at the end, when they only need to wilt.

cauliflower.name: Cauliflower
cauliflower.why_now: Cauliflower is a cool-season crop, and it's sweeter and denser now than at any time in summer. Roasted hard, it turns nutty and golden at the edges.
how_to_choose: Tight, creamy-white curds with no brown spots
Heavy for its size
Fresh, green leaves hugging the head
cauliflower.price_note: Sold by the head. A heavier head for the same price is more cauliflower.

cauliflower.one_thing_to_learn: Cauliflower is mostly water, so it browns only when it has room. Spread it out in one layer, in the air fryer or on a pan, with space around each piece; crowded, it steams and stays pale.

brussels-sprouts.name: Brussels sprouts
brussels-sprouts.why_now: Brussels sprouts are a cool-season crop, and they arrive in November sweeter than they'll be at any other time; a little cold makes them convert starch to sugar. Crisped hard, their outer leaves go brown and nutty and the centers turn tender.
how_to_choose: Small, tight, bright green heads, an inch or so across
Heavy for their size
No yellow outer leaves or black spots
Similar sizes, so they cook evenly
brussels-sprouts.buy_this_much: 1 lb for the salmon and lentils.
brussels-sprouts.price_note: Sold loose by the pound or in bags. Loose lets you pick small, even ones.

brussels-sprouts.storage: In the fridge, unwashed, in a bag, for up to a week. Trim them just before cooking.
brussels-sprouts.one_thing_to_learn: Overcooked Brussels sprouts smell like cabbage because they are cabbage. Cooked hot and fast, cut side down or in moving hot air, they brown before the sulfur builds up.

chicken-thighs.name: Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs
chicken-thighs.tile_uses: The weekend braise, the farro bowls, the crisp chicken, the tinga
chicken-thighs.why_now: There's nothing seasonal about chicken. What changes in November is the weather: the first cool evenings make an hour-long braise appealing again, and bone-in, skin-on thighs are the cut built for it. This is the month's cut.
how_to_choose: Skin that covers the whole thigh, not shrunken back
Pink, plump meat with no gray edges
No liquid pooling in the package
Similar-sized thighs, so they cook evenly
chicken-thighs.buy_this_much: 6, about 2½–3 lbs: the braise, with four left for the farro bowls. Four more for the crisp chicken with white beans or the tinga.
chicken-thighs.price_note: Bone-in, skin-on thighs are one of the cheapest cuts in the case, well below boneless.

chicken-thighs.weekend_use: Seared and braised in the Dutch oven with leeks, fennel, and satsuma. The weekend dish.
chicken-thighs.storage: In the coldest part of the fridge, in the package, for a day or two. Cook within two days of buying.
chicken-thighs.one_thing_to_learn: Thighs are done at 165°F but better at 175–195°F: dark meat has connective tissue that keeps softening as it cooks, so a thigh at 185°F is more tender than one pulled at 165°F, not less. That's true in a braise and in the air fryer.
